title: Indicators of Incident Complexity
cross_references: Common Denominators of Fire Behavior on Tragedy Fires

nodes.text: Determine incident type based on complexity indicators
Type 5: Incident typically terminated quickly, minimal resources needed, no formal planning process

evidence.source_text: Incident is typically terminated or concluded (objective met) within a short time once resources arrive on scene. Formal Incident Planning Process not needed.

nodes.text: Type 4: Incident objectives met within one operational period, limited resources, no formal planning process

evidence.source_text: Incident objectives are typically met within one operational period once resources arrive on scene, but resources may remain on scene for multiple operational periods. Formal Incident Planning Process not needed.

nodes.text: Type 3: Incident extends into multiple operational periods, numerous resources needed, formal planning process initiated

evidence.source_text: Incident typically extends into multiple operational periods. Formal Incident Planning Process is initiated and followed.

nodes.text: Assess span of control and resource supervision
Type 5: IC position filled, single resources supervised by IC

evidence.source_text: Incident Commander (IC) position filled. Single resources are directly supervised by the IC.

nodes.text: Type 4: IC role filled, resources supervised by IC or ICS Leader

evidence.source_text: IC role filled. Resources either directly supervised by the IC or supervised through an ICS Leader position.

nodes.text: Type 3: IC role filled, resources supervised through Operations Section

evidence.source_text: IC role filled. Numerous resources supervised indirectly through the establishment and expansion of the Operations Section and its subordinate positions.
If multiple Type 3 Incident Complexity Indicators are exceeded, consider the next level of incident management support.
